Non-equilibrium resonance scattering in intramolecular charge transport drives conformational changes
radar.summary: Abstract Intramolecular charge transport is conventionally described as proceeding along a static ground-state potential, with the carrier acting as a passive probe of a fixed electronic landscape. Here, using alkanethiolate-based molecular junctions, we show that the carrier itself can drive conformational reorganization once the applied bias brings backbone-delocalized molecular orbitals into the transmission window. Combined electrical and in situ structural measurements resolve a threshold-activated transition to a gauche-defect state coincident with the onset of orbital-mediated transport. We rationalize this coupling through a quantum resonance scattering framework in which accessible orbitals act as scattering potentials that transiently host the injected charge, depositing energy into nuclear motion with an efficiency set by molecule–electrode coupling and Franck–Condon overlap. The framework quantitatively reproduces the measured response and predicts the enhanced behavior of amide-containing junctions. Together, these results suggest that charge-transport–structure feedback can be understood in terms of microscopic parameters governing resonance-mediated energy transfer, and that these parameters may be tuned through chemical design.

radar.title: Agentic Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive and Quantum Aware Network Routing
radar.venue: The International journal of networked and distributed computing
radar.venue_raw: The International journal of networked and distributed computing
radar.summary: Efficient and adaptive routing remains a critical challenge in dynamic network environments due to changing traffic conditions, network congestion, and link failures. Traditional routing approaches, such as Dijkstra and OSPF, rely on static or semi-adaptive mechanisms, which limit their ability to respond to real-time network variations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an Agentic Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (AMARL) framework for intelligent and decentralized routing. In the proposed model, each network node operates as an autonomous agent capable of observing local network conditions, communicating with neighboring agents, and making cooperative routing decisions. A multi-objective reward function is designed to jointly optimize delay, throughput, packet delivery ratio, and packet loss. The framework enables dynamic adaptation to network changes without requiring global recomputation. Extensive simulations are conducted under varying network sizes, traffic conditions, and link failure scenarios. The results demonstrate that the proposed AMARL model achieves significant performance improvements, including up to 45% higher throughput, 35% lower delay, and over 50% reduction in packet loss compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the model maintains higher reliability under link failures and exhibits fast convergence with reduced energy consumption over training episodes. These findings indicate that the integration of agentic intelligence and multi-agent cooperation provides a scalable, adaptive, and efficient solution for next-generation network routing. The proposed framework is particularly suitable for dynamic and large-scale network environments where traditional routing methods fail to perform effectively.

radar.title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
radar.summary: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

radar.title: Multidimensional mechanism design and robust revenue maximization in multi-object auctions
The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
radar.summary: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. radar.title: Strong Nash Equilibria of Core-Selecting Double Auctions
radar.summary: We study core-selecting auctions for double auctions that incorporate package bidding. Unlike in one-sided core-selecting auctions, the core may be empty in more general double auction settings, and truncation strategies need not be amongst a bidder’s best responses. Nevertheless, we establish the existence of a core-selecting auction in which every imputation in the core with respect to true preferences corresponds to a strong Nash equilibrium. Specifically, for any core imputation, there exists a profile of truncation strategies that constitutes a strong Nash equilibrium and induces precisely that imputation.

radar.title: Supervising the search process produces reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents
radar.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are transforming web search by shifting from document ranking to synthesizing answers, and are increasingly deployed as autonomous agentic search systems that iteratively interact with external knowledge sources. Despite this progress, building effective search agents remains challenging because high-quality intermediate search steps are difficult to generate. Previous approaches have primarily relied on outcome supervision, rewarding agents only for producing correct final answers. This often leads to reward hacking and excessive dependence on parametric memory, limiting generalization to out-of-domain tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce RAG-Gym, a framework that shifts supervision from final answers to the search process itself. With RAG-Gym, we systematically investigate architecture design, parameter optimization, and action evaluation, identifying reasoning reflection as a critical capability for search agents. Building on this insight, we propose Re 2 Search++, a process-supervised agent that achieves substantial improvements on multi-hop information-seeking benchmarks, especially in out-of-domain settings. Performance gains are driven primarily by higher-quality search queries rather than answer optimization alone, and the learned search critics transfer across models, including proprietary LLMs. These findings show that supervising the search process produces more reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents.

radar.title: Pure-Strategy Equilibrium in the Generalized First-Price Auction
radar.summary: We revisit the classic result on the (non-)existence of pure-strategy Nash equilibria in the generalized first-price auction for sponsored search advertising and show that the conclusion may be reversed when ads are ranked based on the product of stochastic quality scores and bid amounts rather than solely on the bids or on the product of bids and deterministic quality scores. Moreover, the expected revenue in the pure-strategy equilibrium of the generalized first-price auction may substantially exceed that of the generalized second-price auction, although under some conditions, the relation may also be reversed. radar.title: Robust Auction Design with Support Information
radar.summary: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02703 .

radar.title: Reusability report: multi-sample omics network inference operates in distinct robustness regimes defined by prior knowledge and data availability
radar.summary: Abstract Knowledge-constrained network inference enables the reconstruction of regulatory programmes from high-dimensional biological data, yet the conditions under which shared and context-specific structures can be reliably identified remain poorly understood. Pablo Rodriguez-Mier et al. recently introduced CORNETO, a framework for multi-sample constrained inference. Here we reproduce, evaluate and extend CORNETO in terms of robustness, identifiability and bias–variance trade-offs. Using dynamic haematopoiesis and stable cortical datasets, we systematically assess four network reconstruction paradigms while preserving the original method-specific evaluation procedures and benchmark definitions. We show that multi-sample inference generally improves robustness and reproducibility, although gains in predictive performance depend on biological context and the completeness of the prior network. To enhance stability, we introduce bootstrap aggregation and selective re-expansion strategies that improve consensus robustness and recovery while preserving context-specific signals without modifying the underlying optimization scheme or sacrificing generality. Across datasets and methods, our results reveal distinct inference regimes governed by sample availability, prior knowledge and regularization. Together, these findings position network reconstruction as a regime-dependent learning problem and provide practical principles for robust multi-sample biological network inference.

A diffusion world model and multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for predictive routing in healthcare IoT
radar.summary: Abstract Healthcare Internet of Things (H-IoT) networks support monitoring through wearable sensors, implantable devices, bedside units, mobile gateways, edge nodes, and cloud platforms. Reliable routing is challenging as medical packets are delay-sensitive, while networks face limited energy, mobility, lossy links, congestion, traffic bursts, and sudden node or link failures. This paper presents a diffusion world model and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework for predictive H-IoT routing. The proposed design models the network as a dynamic graph, uses a Temporal Graph Transformer (TGT) to model spatial-temporal dependencies, forecasts link stability, congestion, and failure risk, and uses decentralized agents to select next hops. In ten paired, pre-configured software-emulation scenarios, the executable routing reference prototype achieved measured mean packet delivery ratio of $$56.24\pm 4.75\%$$ , delay of $$42.79\pm 3.34$$ ms, application goodput of $$6.11\pm 0.51$$ kbps, repair overhead of $$0.151\pm 0.024$$ , sensor-radio energy of $$8.94\pm 0.02$$ J, recovery time of $$0.0297\pm 0.0005$$ s, and restricted mean time to first sensor death of $$272.5\pm 44.9$$ s. Source-informed baseline adaptations achieved higher delivery and goodput and lower delay, while the prototype recovered successful routes faster. A separate 20-seed federated-predictor benchmark on emulated patient-group data reported patient-level DP-SGD accountant bound $$(\epsilon ,\delta )=(8,10^{-5})$$ . DP-FedAvg with rehearsal achieved task-1 and task-2 accuracies of $$72.26\pm 1.06\%$$ and $$70.16\pm 0.94\%$$ , respectively, with $$2.24\pm 0.84$$ percentage points of task-1 forgetting.

radar.title: Multi-Agent Cooperative Decision-Making for Connected and Automated Vehicles: A Survey of Methods, Scenarios, and Deployment Challenges
radar.summary: Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) are expected to improve road safety and traffic efficiency, but achieving this remains challenging. This paper presents a methodologically organized survey of cooperative decision-making approaches for CAV systems, tracing their chronological development within each methodological family. The literature is categorized into rule-based and control-theoretic methods; game-theoretic models; single-agent and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approaches; and large language model (LLM)-, vision language model (VLM)-, multimodal large language model (MLLM)-, and foundation-model-based decision support. The reviewed studies address a range of traffic scenarios, including platooning, lane changes, merging, intersections, traffic signals, and mixed-traffic environments. The review compares these methods based on safety, scalability, communication requirements, interpretability, sim-to-real transfer, and mixed-traffic performance. The selected literature illustrates MARL-based approaches to cooperative CAV decision-making; its composition is not used to infer publication growth or the prevalence of methods across the field. Nevertheless, the reviewed MARL methods face challenges concerning safety, communication, scalability, interpretability, and transfer from simulation to real-world deployment. Overall, no single method addresses all the requirements of cooperative CAV systems. Hybrid architectures combining MARL with complementary methods are therefore a promising direction for future CAV systems.

radar.title: Cooling fast and slow: Characterizing the effects of vitrification in cryo-EM and the subsequent recovery of equilibrium populations
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a powerful class of techniques in structural biology with the potential to resolve molecular ensembles, requires that samples be vitrified to protect them from the high vacuum of the electron microscope. However, the effects of vitrification on biomolecular ensembles are unknown. To study them, we carried out extensive molecular dynamics simulations (over 50 ms) of the Trp-cage miniprotein at equilibrium and undergoing rapid cooling. We simulated seven cooling rates spanning three orders of magnitude, with the slowest coolings matching experimental rates. By inspecting molecular mobility and density-temperature trajectories for water with and without protein, we found that water vitrification is unaltered by the protein. To track protein conformation changes, and to relate them to kinetics, we made a Markov State Model (MSM) of Trp-cage from 5.4 ms of equilibrium sampling at 277 K. We observed that MSM states with a characteristic time longer than the duration of the nonequilibrium cooling tend to be more robust to artifacts induced by such cooling. Critically, although we observe that some states vanish in the equilibrium ensemble at 230 K, none do in our nonequilibrium cooled ensembles. To account for these perturbations, we developed a thermodynamic inference framework for recovering equilibrium populations from vitrified ensembles. These results indicate that cryo-EM has the capacity to be an accurate technique for the study of biomolecular ensembles.
radar.summary_short: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a powerful class of techniques in structural biology with the potential to resolve molecular ensembles, requires that samples be vitrified to protect them from the high vacuum of the electron microscope.

radar.title: Uniform Value and Decidability in Ergodic Blind Stochastic Games
radar.summary: We study a class of two-player zero-sum stochastic games known as blind stochastic games, where players neither observe the state nor receive any information about it during the game. A central concept for analyzing long-duration stochastic games is the uniform value. A game has a uniform value v if for every [Formula: see text], Player 1 (resp., Player 2) has a strategy such that, for all sufficiently large n, his average payoff over n stages is at least [Formula: see text] (resp., at most [Formula: see text]). Prior work has shown that the uniform value may not exist in general blind stochastic games. To address this, we introduce a subclass called ergodic blind stochastic games, defined by imposing an ergodicity condition on the state transitions. For this subclass, we prove the existence of the uniform value and provide an algorithm to approximate it, establishing the decidability of the approximation problem. Notably, this decidability result is novel even in the single-player setting of Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs). Furthermore, we show that no algorithm can compute the uniform value exactly, emphasizing the tightness of our result. Finally, we establish that the uniform value is independent of the initial belief. radar.title: EduAgent-RL: A Human-Centered Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Personalized Learning, Adaptive Feedback, and Student Performance Prediction
radar.venue: International Journal of Computer Applications Technology and Research
radar.venue_raw: International Journal of Computer Applications Technology and Research
radar.summary: Personalization in digital learning is often handled through separate components: a knowledge-tracing model estimates what a student knows, a recommender selects learning content, and a conversational tutor provides feedback. These components are not always coordinated as part of a single instructional decision process. Recent reviews of agentic and multi-agent AI in education show rapid growth in this area, but also point to a lack of longitudinal studies and carefully evaluated real-world deployments [3, 12]. To address this gap, we propose EduAgent-RL, a six-agent framework comprising Student Profiling, Learning Analytics, Content Recommendation, Assessment, Feedback, and Teacher/Supervisor agents. The agents are coordinated through centralized-training, decentralized-execution multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), supported by a knowledge-tracing state encoder, retrieval-grounded feedback, and an explicit human-oversight veto. The framework is evaluated on two public benchmarks, OULAD [14] and EdNet [2], against random, collaborative-filtering, classical machine-learning, single-agent RL, and RAG-based LLM tutor baselines. In the pilot evaluation, EduAgent-RL reached an AUROC of 0.83 and NDCG@10 of 0.71 on OULAD, compared with 0.74 AUROC / 0.58 NDCG@10 for the single-agent RL baseline and 0.79 AUROC / 0.63 NDCG@10 for the RAG-based tutor. The ablation results also showed the largest drop in performance when the knowledge-tracing encoder was removed.

radar.title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.
radar.summary_short: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions.

radar.title: dITP shifts the assembly equilibrium of Kongming to activate NAD+ hydrolysis
radar.summary: Abstract The Kongming (Kom) system, consisting of KomA, KomB, and KomC, protects bacteria from phage infection. KomA collaborates with a phage enzyme to generate deoxyinosine 5′-triphosphate (dITP), which activates the KomBC complex to hydrolyze NAD⁺ and trigger cell death. Recent studies propose that dITP activates KomBC through a simple conformational change. Our findings instead reveal a more dynamic mechanism. Without dITP, KomBC complexes exist in equilibrium between tightly packed oligomers and loosely packed filaments, both inactive. Tight packing accumulates unfavorable electrostatic interactions without positioning catalytic residues for NAD⁺ hydrolysis, whereas loose packing relieves these interactions but leaves catalytic residues misaligned. dITP binding at KomB stabilizes tightly packed KomC cores in the filament while aligning catalytic residues. Therefore, a small-molecule signal activates signaling by shifting the assembly equilibrium of higher-order protein complexes toward a catalytically competent state.

Recursive Adversarial Engine: A Stability-Oriented Architecture for Reliable Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems
radar.venue: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications
radar.venue_raw: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications
radar.summary: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems are rapidly migrating from laboratory prototypes to production deployments in finance, scientific research, industrial digital twins, and urban scheduling. As deployment scales, however, a family of systemic pathologies persists: decision oscillation driven by zero-sum agent interactions, cascade propagation of hallucinated content, long-horizon behavioral drift, value misalignment, and unresolved inter-agent conflict. Existing orchestration paradigms, which rely on instruction dispatch, greedy optimization, or static rules, address only shallow coordination and provide no principled mechanism for convergence. This paper proposes the Recursive Adversarial Engine (RAE), a runtime architecture for multi-agent systems organized around three propositions: bounded adversarial interaction supplies the error-detection signal, recursive correction supplies the error-elimination mechanism, and dynamic checks and balances supply the stability guarantee. We specify a four-layer reference architecture comprising adversarial verification, recursive correction, checks-and-balances scheduling, and steady-state output, and we characterize its convergence behavior through a Lyapunov-style stability argument. A qualitative comparison with self-play, multi-agent debate, alignment, and consensus frameworks delineates the paradigm difference. Engineering implications for high-stakes domains, long-horizon robustness, auditability, and middleware integration are analyzed, and open challenges are identified.

radar.title: Public Signals in Affine Network Congestion Games with Uncertain Free-Flow Times
radar.summary: Travel times in road networks are subject to stochastic uncertainty resulting from various parameters. A benevolent mobility service provider observing the actual travel times from data may use its informational advantage to steer the traffic equilibrium in a favorable direction through a processs known as signaling or Bayesian persuasion. Previous work has shown that the underlying signaling problem can be NP-hard to approximate better than [Formula: see text], even for static Wardrop flows with affine cost functions with stochastic offsets. In contrast, we show that in this case, the signaling problem is easy for many networks. First, we tightly characterize the class of single-commodity networks in which full information revelation is always an optimal signaling strategy. Second, we construct a reduction from optimal signaling to computing an optimal collection of active edges for the Wardrop equilibrium. For two states, this allows us to efficiently compute an optimal signaling scheme whenever the number of different active edge sets is bounded by a polynomial in the input size. Using a cell decomposition technique, we extend the approach to a polynomial-time algorithm for multicommodity parallel-edge networks provided that both the number of commodities and states are constant. radar.title: Strategic ignorance and information design
radar.summary: We study information design in strategic settings when agents can publicly refuse to view their private signals. Ignoring the constraints that agents must be willing to view their signals may lead to substantial divergence between the designer’s intent and actual outcomes, even in the case where the designer seeks to maximize the agents’ payoffs. We introduce the appropriate equilibrium concept — ignorance-permissive Bayes correlated equilibrium — and characterize implementable distributions over states and actions. The designer’s optimal response to strategic ignorance generates qualitative properties that standard information design cannot: the designer may provide redundant or even counterproductive information, asymmetric information structures may be strictly optimal in symmetric environments, providing information conditional on players’ viewing choices rather than all at once may hurt the designer, and communication between players may help her. Optimality sometimes requires that players ignore their signals with positive probability.

radar.title: Multiagent Assortment Optimization in Sequential Matching Markets
radar.summary: Motivated by the challenges faced by choice-based matching platforms, in this work, we study a generalization of the two-sided assortment optimization model. Specifically, this model consists of two sides (e.g., customers and suppliers) who have preferences over the opposite side in the form of discrete choice models. A matching is realized through a two-step process where the platform’s decision is to initially present to each agent on one side an assortment of users of the opposite side. The ultimate goal of the platform is to maximize the total expected revenue collected from the matching. Because of the computational complexity of this problem, we focus on the design of approximation algorithms with constant-factor guarantees for the constrained version of the problem under general choice preferences. First, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to draw connections with the literature of submodular optimization and show that one-sided choice-oblivious approaches perform arbitrarily badly. Second, we show that, for the general setting, there exists a two-sided choice-aware randomized algorithm that achieves a [Formula: see text]-approximation factor, which is the best possible. Third, we design an algorithm that is asymptotically optimal when one side follows the well-known multinomial logit (MNL) choice model under the small probability regime. Fourth, we provide a simple and effective algorithm with a [Formula: see text]-approximation guarantee for the unconstrained setting, with both sides following MNL models. Finally, we assess the performance of our proposed methods with a detailed computational study and discuss several extensions. Funding: M. radar.title: Multi-AI agent framework reveals the “oxide gatekeeper” in aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are restricted to small spatiotemporal scales (<500 atoms, picoseconds), while empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited, multiagent framework to make the development and validation of a task-specific machine learning potential (MLP) more traceable and auditable. The workflow coordinates active learning, model evaluation, validation evidence, and human expert review, while leaving scientific interpretation and model-use decisions under researcher control. This collaborative cycle ensures quantum mechanical accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations reveal a temperature-regulated dual-mode oxidation mechanism: At moderate temperatures, the oxide shell acts as a dynamic “gatekeeper,” regulating oxidation through a “breathing mode” of transient nanochannels; above a critical threshold, a “rupture mode” leads to shell failure and rapid combustion. Importantly, we resolve a decades-old controversy by demonstrating that aluminum cation outward diffusion, rather than oxygen transport, dominates mass transfer in studied regimes, with diffusion coefficients consistently exceeding those of oxygen by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude. These results provide an atomistic framework for interpreting ANP reactivity and illustrate how human-audited agentic workflows can make domain-specific reactive MLP development and deployment more reproducible.
radar.summary_short: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive.

Implementation via political parties
radar.summary: We address the implementation of public policies (alternatives) when the feasible set is unknown to the planner. The implementing agents are the political parties, who know the feasible set. They care about the implemented alternative, which reflects their ideology, and their share in parliament and office. They face a mechanism that, given the alternatives proposed by all parties, asks the voters to rank them and determines the chosen alternative and the shares in parliament and office. We identify conditions on parties’ preferences that guarantee the socially optimal policy is the outcome of the unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium of the electoral game played by the parties. The existence of the equilibrium does not require any assumptions about the parties’ ideology. To ensure uniqueness, shares must prevail over ideology: office or parliamentary shares in two-party systems, and strictly office shares in systems with more than two parties.

radar.title: Autonomous biomedical research with an artificial intelligence agent
radar.summary: Biomedical research is increasingly constrained by repetitive, fragmented workflows that slow discovery. We introduce Biomni, a general-purpose biomedical artificial intelligence agent that autonomously executes diverse research tasks. To map the biomedical action space, Biomni’s action-discovery agent mines tools, databases, and protocols from thousands of publications across 25 domains, building a unified agentic environment. Its general-purpose architecture integrates large language model reasoning with retrieval-augmented planning and code-based execution, dynamically composing workflows without predefined templates. Systematic benchmarking shows strong generalization across heterogeneous tasks—causal gene prioritization, drug repurposing, rare-disease diagnosis, microbiome analysis, and molecular cloning—without task-specific tuning. Real-world case studies demonstrate Biomni interpreting multimodal datasets, optimizing protein stability, orchestrating wet-lab instruments, and generating experimentally testable protocols. Biomni envisions artificial intelligence augmenting human scientists and accelerating discovery.
radar.summary_short: Biomedical research is increasingly constrained by repetitive, fragmented workflows that slow discovery. We introduce Biomni, a general-purpose biomedical artificial intelligence agent that autonomously executes diverse research tasks.

radar.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

radar.title: Preserved higher-order mentalising during strategic interactions after medial prefrontal cortex damage
radar.summary: Abstract Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Individuals with medial prefrontal cortex damage achieve similar rewards and use comparable mentalising strategies, but they are slower when making strategic decisions. Computational modelling indicates that this slowing reflects a greater tendency to require evidence before committing to a choice. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identifies medial prefrontal regions linked to altered decision processes rather than mentalising. These findings suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex supports strategic decisions while higher-order mentalising remains intact.

radar.title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
radar.summary: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. radar.title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
radar.summary: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: N. Zhang acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72302053]. radar.title: Nash Equilibrium-Driven Adaptive Behavior in Swarm Intelligence with Self-Organizing Maps
radar.summary: This paper proposes a swarm intelligence model that employs classical boid flocking dynamics combined with non-cooperative game-theoretic methods, specifically Nash Equilibrium, to simulate adaptive decision-making in multi-agent systems. The work leverages a payoff matrix based on fundamental flocking behaviors: cohesion, alignment, and separation, to enable each agent to dynamically optimize its own strategy based on local interactions within the group. The simulation introduces Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) for clustering and behavior adaptation, providing a machine learning perspective on agent categorization and role differentiation. To simulate real-world unpredictability, stochastic noise is used to understand how varying noise levels influence collective alignment and coherence. The results demonstrate the impact of environmental factors on emergent swarm behavior and showcase the benefits of combining machine learning and game theory for adaptive control in distributed systems. This work provides valuable insights into the interplay between noise, decision-making, and flocking dynamics, with broader applications in robotics, swarm intelligence, and autonomous systems.
radar.summary_short: This paper proposes a swarm intelligence model that employs classical boid flocking dynamics combined with non-cooperative game-theoretic methods, specifically Nash Equilibrium, to simulate adaptive decision-making in multi-agent systems.

On the Maximization of Long-Run Conditional Value-at-Risk for Markov Decision Processes
radar.summary: Optimizing Risk-Seeking Sequential Decisions via Conditional Value-at-Risk Decision makers may exhibit risk-seeking preferences in finance, energy operations, and stochastic resource management, yet corresponding Markov decision process (MDP) theories remain underdeveloped. In this paper, “On the Maximization of Long-Run CVaR for Markov Decision Processes,” Xia, Yu, and Wu investigate infinite-horizon MDPs maximizing long-run conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) for instantaneous rewards. They prove optimality for stationary randomized policies and show deterministic policies may fail; an optimal policy randomizes over at most two actions. By converting the original problem into a minimax saddle point formulation, the authors develop solvable linear programming and globally convergent gradient descent algorithms. Results are further extended to joint mean-CVaR optimization and validated on real-world microgrid scheduling data. This work fills gaps for risk-seeking MDPs and delivers practical computation tools for tail-oriented sequential decision making.

radar.title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
radar.summary: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. This paper was accepted by Miguel Villas-Boas, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03426 .

radar.title: Maintaining Coordination in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Under Pairwise Asynchronous Link Failures Through Cached-Message Reuse
radar.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) relies on communication when local observations are incomplete. Pairwise asynchronous link failures interrupt different directed links at different times and remove part of the information used for coordination. This paper studies whether agents can maintain coordination by reusing the latest message received from each unavailable neighbor. We propose Temporal Graph-based Neighbor Aggregation with Age-Penalized Communication (TGN-APC). Each agent stores one message per neighbor and limits reuse by message age. TGN-APC reuses a valid cached message and subtracts an age penalty from its attention score. We evaluate the method on the Vectorized Multi-Agent Simulator Navigation task with ten independent training seeds. Cache reuse significantly improves return and team completion over direct one-hop communication under short and long failure bursts. An age penalty coefficient of 0.10 does not significantly improve on cache reuse without an age term. Matched validation-based coefficient selection shows no significant difference between score penalization and exponential content scaling after multiple-testing correction. A two-hop current-message variant gives the highest long-burst return, but it uses about 83% more active transmissions than TGN-APC. These results support cached-message reuse for the tested task and failure model. They do not establish a separate performance gain from the selected age penalty.

radar.title: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Multi-agent systems of large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding across domains, introducing dynamics not captured by single-agent evaluations. Yet, existing work has mostly contrasted the behavior of a single agent with that of a collective of fixed size, leaving open a central question: How does group size shape dynamics? Here, we move beyond this dichotomy and systematically explore outcomes across the full range of group sizes. We focus on multi-agent misalignment, building on recent evidence that interacting LLMs playing a simple coordination game can generate collective biases absent in individual models. First, we show that collective bias is a deeper phenomenon than previously assessed: Interaction can amplify individual biases, introduce new ones, or override model-level preferences. Second, we demonstrate that group size affects the dynamics in a nonlinear way, revealing model-dependent dynamical regimes. Finally, we develop a mean-field analytical approach and show that, above a critical population size, simulations converge to deterministic predictions that expose the basins of attraction of competing equilibria. These findings establish group size as a key driver of multi-agent dynamics and highlight the need to consider population-level effects when deploying LLM-based systems at scale.

radar.title: A Parametric Active-Set Algorithm for Solving Monotone Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problems
radar.summary: We present a fast active-set algorithm for the solution of monotone linear-quadratic generalized Nash equilibrium problems (GNEPs) with shared affine inequality and equality constraints. The algorithm, which we call gPAQ, is an adaptation of the parametric active-set method proposed by Best (1996) and extended in qpOASES by Ferreau et al. (2014) to solve convex quadratic programs. Under strong monotonicity, we show that the same active-set strategy applies. We handle the case of merely monotone problems by using gPAQ as the inner solver within proximal-point iterations. To solve strongly monotone convex nonlinear GNEPs, we propose a Newton-type iterative scheme, which we call gPAN, which iteratively linearizes the nonlinear problem and solves the resulting LQ-GNEP subproblems using gPAQ. We show in numerical examples that the proposed algorithms are significantly faster than existing methods.

radar.title: Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange
radar.summary: Unlocking Value Through Nonprofit Resource Sharing Nonprofit organizations often operate under tight budgets while idle equipment, unused space, and shareable skills and expertise are frequently underutilized, with existing resource exchanges in the nonprofit sector limited to bilateral barter or relatively homogeneous resources. In “Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange,” Huang et al. propose Sharing With a Purpose (SWAP), a resource-sharing system that enables nonprofits to exchange heterogeneous resources without monetary payments. SWAP combines an auction-based process, SWAPcredit valuation, and integer optimization to facilitate multilateral exchanges, allowing nonprofits to obtain needed resources by contributing resources of their own. The authors implement this market design through the SWAP Hub, a digital platform deployed with nonprofit communities in multiple regions. Through repeated exchange episodes, participating organizations have shared not only physical assets but also a wide range of skills, services, and expertise, including marketing, management, event planning, and organizational development. The study demonstrates how innovative market design can unlock latent value in community resources, alleviate resource constraints, and encourage new connections and collaboration among nonprofit organizations.

radar.title: Posterior-conditioned multi-agent reinforcement learning for adaptive cyber defense
radar.summary: Cyber defense increasingly relies on teams of autonomous agents that must act under partial observability while adversaries shift tactics and objectives over time. Standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods often overfit to fixed threat models, whereas worst-case robust training can be overly conservative and fail to use observations about the active attack regime. We propose posterior-conditioned MARL, a context-aware framework formulated as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP). In addition to its local history, each defender conditions its decentralized policy on a shared attack-context belief, a probabilistic representation of the attack regime inferred online from recent multi-agent interaction trajectories. This belief provides a low-dimensional representation of evolving adversarial behavior and enables coordinated adaptation during execution without test-time policy optimization or retraining. We provide a performance analysis that quantifies how errors in the inferred attack-context belief translate into degraded long-term defense performance, clarifying the tradeoff between robustness and adaptivity. Experiments on the Cyber Autonomy Gym for Experimentation (CybORG) CAGE-4 cyber operations testbed show improved mission reward and adaptability, particularly under mixed and switching attack conditions, compared with domain-randomized, worst-case robust, and hierarchical defense baselines.

radar.title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals
radar.summary: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.

radar.title: TradeGauntlet: Evaluating Compliance Controls for Autonomous Trading Agents
radar.summary: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.
radar.summary_short: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost.

authors: Artificial Hyperintelligence, Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Ŋeirū ∿ Sihā II develops a mathematical framework for choosing small, equal-weight training sets while controlling their effect on learning. Its central contributions are an obstruction to extending the planar selection law into higher dimensions, an exact solution of a complete family of fixed-probability geometric minimax problems, and explicit certificates connecting data selection to quadratic training, gradient reuse, and repeated learning updates. The release contains a 41-page, self-contained manuscript, the complete 36-file original research package, editable LaTeX sources, exact-arithmetic algorithms, matching upper and lower certificates, reproducible figures, and verification reports. 1. The problem: how much learning can a small selected set preserve? The geometric setting addresses Question 1 of “Open Problem: Data Selection for Regression Tasks,” presented at COLT 2025. A teacher observes a dataset and chooses exactly n original examples, allowing repetitions. The learner returns their equal-weight mean h. Writing μ for the full-data mean and V for its variance, the squared-loss identity is L_full(h) = V + ||h − μ||². The central quantity F(d,n) is the worst-case ratio between the best selected learner’s full-data loss and V in dimension d, for nonzero-variance datasets. The manuscript reproduces the supplied planar theorem F(2,n) = 2n/(2n−1), then develops the higher-dimensional theory and its learning consequences. 2. An all-budget higher-dimensional obstruction For every dimension k ≥ 4 and selection budget n ≥ 2, the manuscript establishes F(k,n) ≥ 1 + B(k,n), where B(k,n) = [2n(k−2) − (k−3) − sqrt((k−3)[2n(n−2)(k−2) + (k−3)])] / (k n²). In dimension four, the expression simplifies to B(4,n) = [4n − 1 − sqrt(4n² − 8n + 1)] / (4n²), and satisfies B(4,n) > 1/(2n−1) for every n ≥ 2. Consequently, the planar formula fails at every nontrivial budget in every dimension at least four. The construction combines a frequent anchor with rare regular-simplex vertices. The proof reduces all possible selections to their integer count patterns and optimizes the resulting geometric family. Rational approximation connects continuously optimized masses to finite empirical datasets. A fully explicit witness consists of 128 integer-coordinate observations in four dimensions. At budget three, its exact optimal full-data loss ratio is 13810/11457, strictly greater than 6/5. Exhaustive rational-arithmetic checks accompany this witness. The obstruction also gives an asymptotic lower coefficient liminf as n → ∞ of n[F(k,n)−1] ≥ [2(k−2) − sqrt(2(k−2)(k−3))] / k. This coefficient exceeds 1/2 for k > 4 and approaches 2−sqrt(2) as dimension grows. 3. Exact minimax for an entire symmetric mass family The principal exact result fixes the probability vector p = (1−t, t/k, …, t/k), with one anchor, k equally probable rare atoms, k ≥ 2, and 0 < t < 1. The support locations may vary arbitrarily. For every positive integer budget n, the worst normalized squared mean error over these geometries equals C(k,n,t) = max over 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1 of min over r = 0,…,n of [λ a_r + (1−λ)b_r], where a_r = (r/n − t)² / [t(1−t)], b_r = s_r(k−s_r) / [(k−1)n²t], s_r = r mod k. The geometric optimization therefore becomes a finite game between axial and transverse modes. The result supplies both a matching normalized Gram-matrix witness and a randomized selection policy. An optimal policy uses at most two balanced rare-count types; a type specifies a total number of rare draws and can represent multiple actual count vectors. A residue-class dominance argument leaves at most min(k,n+1) candidate totals. The exact solver uses O(min(k,n+1)³) scalar arithmetic operations, excluding integer bit costs and optional full-count verification or lottery expansion. For k = 5, n = 4, and t = 1/2, the exact normalized squared mean error is 3/20. A matching policy chooses three anchor copies and one uniformly selected rare atom with probability 3/5, or two anchor copies and two uniformly selected distinct rare atoms with probability 2/5. Its expected squared mean error is exactly (3/20)V for every geometry with these masses. A matching lower certificate proves optimality for this fixed profile. 4. Constructive selection, constraints, and unbiasedness The manuscript also provides constructive upper guarantees in every finite affine rank. Its coefficient U_r(n) is strictly below 1/n for finite rank r and n ≥ 2. A complementary fractional-residual construction gives instance-specific certificates and O(n⁻²) squared mean error for a fixed finite geometry. Fixed-geometry asymptotics and budget-dependent worst-case asymptotics are distinguished explicitly. A general finite admissible-count formulation accommodates repetition caps, mandatory or forbidden observations, category quotas, and rational linear costs. Upper certificates use matrix inequalities for lotteries over legal selections. Lower certificates use centered normalized Gram matrices and complete coverage of the legal count set. Exact primal–dual equality in this general formulation allows ambient dimension up to support size minus one; smaller fixed dimensions impose an additional rank constraint. The package includes an exact rational positive-semidefiniteness checker based on Schur complements. It checks supplied certificates, including singular cases, without floating-point tolerances. A separate theorem establishes that the best universal expected squared mean error coefficient for mean-unbiased equal-weight selectors is exactly 1/n. This identifies a substantive boundary between optimized biased selection and unbiased stochastic estimation. 5. Quadratic training with varying curvature For convex per-example quadratic losses, let H_i be the individual Hessians, H their positive-definite full-data average, and θ* the full-data optimizer. Define normalized curvature and residual-gradient features by A_i = H^(−1/2) H_i H^(−1/2), r_i = H^(−1/2)(H_i θ* − b_i), M = E[||A_i − I||_F²], G = E[||r_i||²]. If c is a valid selection coefficient for the joint lifted curvature–residual features and cM < 1, an equal-weight selection exists whose empirical-risk minimizer θ_selected satisfies J(θ_selected) − J(θ*) ≤ cG / [2(1−sqrt(cM))²]. The proof jointly controls curvature distortion and residual-gradient error, then optimizes their relative weighting. The applicable coefficient depends on the lifted feature rank. The construction assumes access to the full Hessian, optimizer, and required normalized features, so their preparation costs remain part of the learning procedure. 6. Certified replay, gradient reuse, and recursive error control Stored gradient and higher-derivative summaries receive explicit reuse regions and approximation-error certificates. radar.title: Single and multi-winner auctions with performance obligation
radar.summary: Auctioning access rights to private providers through competitive tendering has become a central instrument for governments to regulate markets and public services. While efficient in allocating licenses, such auctions may generate monopolistic market structures with adverse effects on consumer welfare. We experimentally evaluate two policy interventions to mitigate these outcomes: introducing post-tender competition and imposing minimum production obligations on winning firms. Our results show that performance obligations substantially improve welfare by raising output and consumer surplus, albeit at the cost of reduced auction revenue. Extending the design with additional treatments, we demonstrate that genuine competition yields even stronger welfare gains. These findings highlight a trade-off between government revenue and consumer welfare in auction design. We conclude that while obligations are an effective tool to counter monopoly distortions, sustaining competition remains essential to maximise total surplus at the market level.

radar.title: Game-Theoretic Analysis of RIS-Assisted Challenge-Response PLA - Part II: Partial Channel Knowledge
radar.summary: We consider a physical layer authentication scenario in which a legitimate user (Alice) communicates with an authenticator (Bob) through a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), controlled by Bob. An attacker (Trudy) aims to impersonate Alice by suitably precoding her messages and still transmitting them through the RIS. This two-part study analyzes this attack-defense interaction between Bob and Trudy under perfect (Part I) and partial (Part II) channel knowledge by all the agents. Part I formulates the joint RIS selection and precoder design under perfect channel knowledge as a finite zero-sum game, establishing exact channel subspace conditions for attack indistinguishability alongside equilibrium mixed strategies. Part II extends the defense to incomplete channel information, where each agent observes only its own channel, by formulating a finite-action Bayesian game and characterizing the resulting Bayesian Nash equilibrium. Simulations in geometric and 3GPP TR 38.901 UMi-NLOS channels reveal that authentication performance is governed by available spatial degrees of freedom, channel correlation, and operating signal-to-noise ratio. The proposed equilibrium strategies effectively balance communication rate and security, outperforming conventional benchmark policies.

radar.title: A Dynamical Systems and Game-Theoretic Framework for Quantitative Ethics: Means of Production, Evolutionary Demography, and the Mathematical Necessity of Human-AI Symbiosis
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Classical moral philosophy treats good, evil, and justice as subjective or culturally relative concepts, resisting objective quantification. Grounded in evolutionary biology and dynamical systems theory, this paper establishes a mathematical framework for quantitative ethics by defining universal moral polarity as the directional gradient of a global survival potential function Φ(S, N), where S denotes biodiversity (inclusive of humanity) and N represents human population. Within this formulation, historical variations in normative justice are derived as constrained optimal control policies governed by the carrying capacity K(M) of prevailing means of production M, with institutional shifts modeled as deterministic saddle-node bifurcations. Analyzing the contemporary structural transition toward autonomous artificial intelligence (M_AI) as of 2026, we prove that capital-monopolized automation induces a coupled dual catastrophe: ecological overshoot and a microeconomic fertility trap yielding a corner Nash equilibrium of zero reproduction (n_i* = 0). Finally, we demonstrate that structuring human-AI interaction as a polycentric Decentralized Autonomous Commons (DAC) with super-linear co-production synergy (α + β > 1) eliminates governance friction and socializes reproductive costs, establishing Bio-Tech Symbiosis as the unique stable attractor aligning individual rationality with long-term species survival.

radar.title: An Analysis of Zero-Sum Game Agent Training Based on Large Language Models and Self-Play Mechanisms
radar.summary: This paper carries out a review of competitive agent training under zero‑sum game settings, analysing persistent drawbacks found in traditional self‑play reinforcement learning, including inflexible decision‑making policies and weak long‑horizon reasoning capacity. Game agents built purely upon large language models are incapable of sustaining iterative upgrades amid ongoing adversarial contests. Accordingly, the present work investigates viable integration schemes that unite large language models and self‑play training systems. It first lays out the definition of zero‑sum games, illustrates standard self‑play training workflows, and revisits fundamental algorithms from game theory. Four practical integration patterns are classified, namely auxiliary policy generation, reward evaluation optimisation, accumulation of adversarial experience, and the construction of diversified training opponents. Relying on theoretical formula derivation and comparative experimental statistics, this paper evaluates widely adopted modern frameworks against five core benchmarks: reasoning performance, training productivity, generalisation capability, computational expenditure, and training stability, so as to compare their distinct strengths and weaknesses. Evaluation findings indicate that each standalone integration paradigm bears intrinsic flaws. Frameworks adopting dynamically‑generated opponents deliver optimal generalisation performance, while optimised reward mechanisms enable the fastest training convergence. Nonetheless, all hybrid training architectures confront common bottlenecks such as LLM hallucination, prohibitive computational overhead, and oscillating gradient signals during model training. This review identifies several high‑potential research directions: dynamic multi‑module collaborative structures, streamlined self‑play workflows, retrieval‑augmented technologies to restrain hallucination, as well as the development of general‑purpose game agents. The outcomes of this analysis can supply theoretical references for future advances in adversarial decision‑making artificial intelligence.

radar.title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
radar.summary: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.

radar.title: OpenLayout: An Open and Agentic-Driven Platform for Holistic VLSI Physical Design and Benchmarking
radar.summary: Physical design automation of very large-scale integrated circuits (VLSI) has made significant strides, progressing from single-stage placement and routing toward increasingly integrated full-flow implementation. Yet, existing approaches struggle with the vast design space optimization (DSO) arising from diverse technology nodes, circuit designs, and varied constraints. The substantial runtime of physical-design tools further exacerbates this challenge, leaving industrial workflows heavily dependent on experienced engineers to navigate the design space and achieve power, performance, and area (PPA) targets, incurring significant engineering effort. We argue that large language models (LLMs) with strong reasoning capabilities, enriched with distilled human design expertise, offer a promising path toward efficient and automated DSO. Unlike traditional algorithms, LLMs can interpret complex design contexts and naturally incorporate human expertise expressed in natural language for reasoning, acting, observing, and adapting throughout the design process, a capability that conventional optimization methods cannot exploit. To this end, we present OpenLayout, an agentic platform that leverages multi-agent collaboration with embedded design knowledge to enable self-iterative DSO. We further introduce OpenLayout-Bench, a benchmark targeting advanced technology nodes with commercial EDA tools to systematically evaluate physical design automation capabilities of LLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that OpenLayout achieves state-of-the-art performance, with approximately 20% accuracy improvement over baseline methods. Our work is open-sourced at https://github.com/fenggev56/OpenLayout

radar.title: A Better Cycle-Breaker for Direct Democracy?
radar.summary: When a counter-proposal is made to an initiative to change the Swiss constitution, the citizenry makes three binary majority choices: the initiative versus the status quo, the counter-proposal versus the status quo, and the initiative versus the counter-proposal as a tie-breaker. If the three majority choices form a cycle, the current rule selects the alternative that beats the status quo. This rule may lead to strategic voting. We suggest breaking cycles differently by choosing the middle alternative in case of a cycle, which will normally be the counter-proposal. More precisely, we study Condorcet-consistent pairwise majority voting procedures when preferences are single-peaked and their distribution is common knowledge. We then show that whenever a strong Nash equilibrium exists, its outcome is the same as under sincere voting, and we characterize the cycle-breaking defaults for which sincere voting is itself a strong Nash equilibrium. In particular, among procedures that use the same default for both possible cycles, the middle alternative is the unique common default.

radar.title: Sustainable Multi-Zone Greenhouse Fertigation Through Reliability-Aware Sensing, Spatiotemporal Graph Learning, and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: With protected agriculture increasingly developing toward large-scale, multi-zone, and intelligent production, reducing water and fertilizer consumption, drainage losses, and energy waste while maintaining crop yield, product quality, and long-term economic profitability has become an important challenge for sustainable greenhouse production. To address sensor abnormalities, spatial heterogeneity among irrigation zones, competition for shared hydraulic resources, and the limited ability of conventional control strategies to jointly optimize resource efficiency and economic performance, a sensor-driven spatiotemporal graph multi-agent reinforcement learning framework, termed SensorGraph-FertiMARL, is proposed for state sensing, response prediction, and sustainable coordinated fertigation optimization in multi-zone greenhouses. Reliable zone-level states are first obtained through sensor-reliability gating, missing-state reconstruction, and multi-relational graph fusion incorporating spatial, hydraulic, and microclimatic relationships. An action-conditioned fertigation–yield–quality–profit digital twin is then constructed to jointly predict root-zone responses, resource consumption, marketable yield, product quality, and net profit associated with candidate control actions. Finally, graph-based multi-agent proximal policy optimization (Graph-MAPPO) with capacity, safety, and fairness constraints is employed to coordinate fertigation allocation among multiple zones under shared pump, main-pipeline, and nutrient-solution resource constraints. Evaluated through rigorous offline digital-twin simulation and replay testing calibrated against complete multi-stage historical dataset records from an eight-zone commercial greenhouse, experimental results show that the proposed method reduced water and fertilizer use to 75.8% and 78.3% (achieving water and fertilizer saving rates of 24.2% and 21.7%), respectively, relative to the uniform timer-based control baseline, while decreasing the drainage rate to 7.2%. The Grade-A product rate increased to 84.6%, net profit reached 138.9% of the baseline level (a +38.9% net-profit improvement), return on investment (ROI) reached 1.94, and the stress-violation rate was limited to 2.9%. For state sensing and digital-twin prediction, the sensor-state reconstruction mean absolute error (MAE) and coefficient of determination (R2) were 0.036 and 0.918, respectively; the water-content prediction MAE was 0.041, the electrical conductivity (EC) prediction root mean squared error (RMSE) was 0.119, and the drainage prediction mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was 8.7%. In addition, the R2 for marketable-yield prediction reached 0.912, the macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1) score for quality-grade prediction reached 0.851, the R2 for net-profit prediction reached 0.904, the mean prediction interval width (MPIW) was 0.142, and the prediction interval coverage probability (PICP) reached 0.931. These results demonstrate that SensorGraph-FertiMARL can simultaneously achieve water and fertilizer conservation, drainage reduction, operational-risk control, and economic improvement while maintaining marketable production and quality, thereby providing an effective intelligent optimization approach for resource-efficient, environmentally sustainable, and economically viable greenhouse production.

radar.title: Stochastic Games with Distributional Entropy Objectives
radar.summary: We introduce \emph{stochastic games with distributional entropy objectives}, two-player zero-sum games whose configurations are probability distributions over the states of a finite arena and whose stage reward is Shannon entropy. Over an infinite discounted horizon, MIN seeks to concentrate the distribution, while MAX seeks to disperse it. Because entropy is nonlinear, it matters whether strategic and transition randomness are averaged before entropy is evaluated or sampled first. We formalise three resulting semantics: averaged-distribution, sampled-profile, and sampled-transition. This semantic choice fundamentally changes the game-theoretic structure. Averaged-distribution games need not be determined, even on a four-state deterministic arena, whereas both sampled semantics are determined and admit optimal stationary randomised strategies. We give contractive Bellman characterisations and convergent finite-horizon approximations for the upper and lower averaged values and the two sampled values. Moreover, even the lower value under averaged-distribution semantics dominates the value under either sampled semantics, while the sampled-profile and sampled-transition values are incomparable in general. For fixed rational discount and positive rational promise gap, the averaged-distribution (upper and lower value) gap problems and both sampled gap problems lie in PSPACE; for a single entropy minimiser, the averaged and sampled-profile problems lie in NP. Finally, under all three semantics, entropy optimisation is NP-hard to approximate within a suitable fixed additive constant, already for deterministic one-player games, where pure memoryless strategies are optimal.
radar.summary_short: We introduce \emph{stochastic games with distributional entropy objectives}, two-player zero-sum games whose configurations are probability distributions over the states of a finite arena and whose stage reward is Shannon entropy.

radar.title: SELFISH AND COOPERATIVE BEHAVIOUR IN NONATOMIC CONGESTION GAMES
radar.summary: The paper examines the influence of cooperative behavior on the players' population assignment among alternatives in a non-atomic congestion game with affine cost functions. The formulation of the congestion game is proposed in which the player population consists not only of individualists but also of players acting in the interests of a cooperating group. In this formulation, a Nash equilibrium is explicitly obtained, allowing us to analyze the interdependence and interaction of strategies for assigning players among alternatives in a non-atomic congestion game with groups of cooperating players. It is proven that the number of alternatives sought by cooperating players is always no less than the number sought by individualists. Moreover, when groups of cooperating players compete in a congestion game, a larger number of alternatives can only be sought by a larger group. Finally, it is shown that the average payoff of a cooperating player is never greater than the payoff of an individualist.
